title: VRAC coordinates the trade-off between nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes against inflammation

paper_content.abstract: Enterocytes mediate both nutrient absorption and antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion while constantly exposed to osmotic fluctuations. However, the role of volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC), a key osmo-sensitive ion channel, in enterocytes and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains unclear. Here, we show that intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific knockout of LRRC8A, the essential VRAC subunit, exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer. VRAC deficiency specifically disrupts enterocyte maturation and zonation, expanding AMP-producing enterocytes while reducing enterocytes responsible for nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism emerges as the most affected nutrient pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, with reduced Adh1, Aldh1a2 expression and aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. Supplementation with retinoic acid reversed inflammation caused by VRAC deficiency. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, while administration of Lactobacillus species effectively restored microbial balance and alleviated inflammation. This study delineates the role of VRAC in balancing nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes to safeguard gut homeostasis.
paper_content.introduction:
Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic, relapsing disorder of the gastrointestinal tract and represents key risk factors for inflammation-associated colorectal cancer (CAC)1,2. Although the precise pathogenesis of IBD remains unclear, multiple factors have been implicated, including dysregulated immune responses, alterations in the gut microbiota, genetic predisposition, and environmental triggers.

Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs)—comprising stem cells, enterocytes, goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells, Paneth cells, and tuft cells—form a physical and functional barrier that not only separates luminal contents from the underlying mucosa but also regulates nutrient absorption and barrier integrity3. A growing body of evidence highlights the critical role of intestinal epithelial dysfunction in the initiation and progression of IBD, serving as a key interface that links luminal insults to aberrant immune activation and chronic inflammation4–6. Dysfunction in IEC differentiation, IEC-microbe interactions, or IEC-immune crosstalk plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of IBD or colorectal cancer7,8.

Among different types of IECs, enterocytes, which constitute approximately 90% of IECs, are the most prominent type and are responsible for nutrient and water absorption, and antimicrobial defense9,10. Importantly, enterocytes in both the small intestine and colon exhibit a spatially organized transcriptional and functional zonation pattern along the crypt–surface axis11–14. At the crypt base, enterocytes predominantly express genes involved in host defense, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and metal-ion transporters. As cells migrate upward, mid-zone enterocytes specialize in amino acid, vitamin, and carbohydrate absorption, while surface-located enterocytes are primarily responsible for lipid uptake11,12. Although nutrient malabsorption has been closely linked to the development and progression of IBD, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate enterocyte function in nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense—especially under inflammatory stress—remain poorly defined.

Mammalian cells need to regulate their volume by transporting ions and small organic osmolytes via ion channels and transporters to counteract osmotic swelling or shrinkage13,14. The volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) plays a pivotal role in restoring normal cell volume by mediating the efflux of chloride in response to cellular swelling14. VRAC is a heteromeric channel composed of subunits from the LRRC8 protein family (LRRC8A-E), with LRRC8A (also named SWELL1) being essential and required to heteromerize with at least one other subunit (LRRC8B–E) to form a functional channel15,16. In addition to transporting Cl−, VRAC is capable of transporting a wide variety of substances, including inositol, taurine, amino acids, and immune metabolites17–21. Notably, the specific heteromeric composition of VRAC subunits determines the channel’s distinct biophysical properties and physiological roles22,23. Serving as the largest barrier surface in the body, IECs are constantly exposed to significant osmolarity alterations caused by dietary intake, digestion, and various pathophysiological conditions24,25. However, little is known about the role of VRAC in regulating IEC function and its involvement in intestinal inflammation. In this study, we systematically investigated VRAC function in IECs using a combination of IEC-specific Lrrc8a conditional knockout mice and multiple inflammation models, including dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)- and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced colitis, as well as the azoxymethane (AOM)/DSS-induced inflammation-associated cancer model. We reveal that epithelial VRAC plays a critical role in preserving intestinal homeostasis under inflammatory conditions. Furthermore, deletion of Lrrc8d, encoding another key subunit of VRAC, also aggravated colitis, underscoring the functional importance of LRRC8A/8D-containing VRAC complexes in IECs. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that VRAC is specifically required for enterocyte maturation and zonation, as shown by scRNA-seq and organoid analyses. VRAC deficiency results in enterocyte reprogramming toward antimicrobial defense at the expense of nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism was the most impaired nutrient absorption pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, and its supplementation alleviated inflammation. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, notably reducing Lactobacillus species, while Lactobacillus administration mitigated inflammation caused by IEC VRAC loss. Collectively, our findings identify VRAC as a critical rheostat that coordinates nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes, thereby maintaining intestinal homeostasis during inflammation.
paper_content.results:
Intestinal VRAC loss exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer
To investigate the potential role of VRAC in IEC homeostasis and intestinal inflammation, we analyzed the expression levels of VRAC subunits in healthy individuals and IBD patients using published RNA-seq data from the GEO database. The data demonstrate that the expression of LRRC8A, the essential subunit of VRAC, was increased in the colon of IBD patients compared to healthy donors (Fig. S1A, B). LRRC8D, another key VRAC subunit, also exhibited high expression relative to other VRAC components, which indicates a potential link between VRAC and the development of IBD. Besides, immunohistochemistry showed slightly enhanced epithelial LRRC8A staining in CD biopsies, and this was accompanied by a modest increase in overall LRRC8A protein levels (Fig. S1C, D).

To determine the effects of VRAC in IECs and IBD, we generated IEC-specific Lrrc8a-knockout mice by crossing Lrrc8afl/fl mice with Villin1 (Vil1)-Cre transgenic mice26. These mice were hereinafter referred to as Lrrc8aΔIEC mice, whereas littermate Lrrc8afl/fl mice were used as WT controls (Fig. S2A). The loss of Lrrc8a in IECs of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was validated by qPCR and Western blot (Fig. S2B, C). The body weight, water intake, and spleen weight were similar between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2D–F). Besides, the deletion of LRRC8A in IECs had no significant effect on fecal weight or water content (Fig. S2G). Histology and tight-junction markers of the colon and distal ileum also showed no overt abnormalities between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2H–K). These suggest VRAC in IECs is dispensable for the functionality of intestinal epithelia in the steady state. To elucidate the potential role of VRAC in IECs upon inflammatory stress, WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice were then subjected to DSS-induced colitis27. Of note, greater body weight loss and higher disease activity index (DAI) upon challenge with 1.5% or 2.5% DSS was observed in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 1A, B). The colon length of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was much shorter than that of WT mice upon DSS challenge, indicating more severe inflammatory damage (Fig. 1C). Moreover, the lethality in the Lrrc8aΔIEC mice subjected to 3% DSS was significantly increased (Fig. 1D). Furthermore, Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited heightened epithelial erosion and inflammation, along with a pronounced reduction in mucus-secreting goblet cells after DSS treatment (Fig. 1E, F). To further validate the role of VRAC in intestinal inflammation, we established a TNBS-induced colitis model, which closely mimics the immunepathology of CD. Lrrc8aΔIEC mice also exhibited reduced colon length and enhanced inflammation, together with greater body weight loss (Fig. S3). Taken together, these findings suggest that intestinal VRAC plays a vital protective role in the development and progression of colitis.

VRAC and cell volume regulation have been shown to transport specific immune metabolites such as cGAMP and itaconate, thereby playing key roles in both innate and adaptive immunity28,29. Thereby, Lrrc8afl/fl mice were also crossed with LysM-Cre mice or CD4-Cre mice, to achieve conditional ablation of Lrrc8a in myeloid cells (Lrrc8aΔLysM) or T cells (Lrrc8aΔCD4), respectively (Fig. S2A). However, the results demonstrate that mice lacking Lrrc8a in either myeloid cells or T cells exhibited comparable weight loss, DAI, colon shortening, and histopathological features compared to control littermates upon DSS challenge (Fig. 1G–L). These findings emphasize that it is intestinal epithelial VRAC, rather than immune cell-intrinsic VRAC, that plays a critical role in protecting against intestinal inflammation.

IBD is a well-established risk factor for the development of inflammation-associated colorectal cancer30. We further explored the role of intestinal VRAC in the development of inflammation-associated colorectal cancer by using AOM combined with low concentrations of DSS (1%), given that Lrrc8aΔIEC mice tended to succumb to DSS exposure. Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited significantly more body weight loss during DSS treatment (Fig. 2A). At day 80 post-AOM-DSS treatment, colons of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice developed a markedly increased tumor burden, including higher tumor numbers and larger tumor sizes (Fig. 2B–D). Histological analysis revealed a greater extent of inflammation and epithelial hyperplasia in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 2E–G). Taken together, our data demonstrate a crucial role of intestinal VRAC in protecting the intestine against inflammatory stimuli, including colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer.

Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited enhanced inflammatory responses and intestinal epithelial damage
Next, we performed bulk RNA-seq analysis using colon RNAs from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice after DSS challenge. In Lrrc8aΔIEC mice, 110 genes were notably downregulated, while 355 genes were significantly upregulated (|log FC|>1; adjusted P<0.05) (Fig. 3A). Gene ontology (GO) analysis by Enrichr showed a significant upregulation associated with inflammatory response genes, neutrophil migration, and antimicrobial response. Whereas, genes involved in lipid transport and ion transport exhibited a noticeable reduction in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 3B). Inflammatory genes (e.g., Cxcl10, Il6) were significantly increased, as confirmed via qPCR, in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice subjected to DSS or AOM-DSS treatment (Fig. 3C, E). Besides, the expression levels of AMPs such as calprotectin subunits S100a8 and S100a9, were markedly elevated in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 3D). Moreover, increased apoptosis and reduced epithelial cell proliferation in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice were observed by enhanced staining for TUNEL along with decreased staining for the proliferation marker Ki67, demonstrating impaired intestinal healing (Fig. 3F). Thus, the loss of VRAC results in enhanced inflammatory and antimicrobial responses while decreasing ion and lipid transport under intestinal inflammatory stress.

Given the central role of intestinal barrier dysfunctions in intestinal inflammation, we examined whether IEC VRAC deficiency compromised the barrier integrity by analyzing the distribution or expression of tight-junction protein zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), Occludin, and Claudin-2. Consistently, colons from Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited notably disrupted tight junctions (Fig. 3G), suggesting a compromised mucosal barrier in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice. This was further confirmed by the elevated fluorescence in the serum of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice fed with FITC-labeled dextran (MW 4000), indicative of colonic leakage (Fig. 3H). The data reveal that VRAC in IECs is crucial for maintaining the intestinal barrier and provides significant protection against colitis and CAC.

Intestinal VRAC is specifically required for enterocyte maturation and zonation
To explore the underlying mechanism by which IEC VRAC protects against intestinal inflammation, we analyzed different VRAC subunits in IECs using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of human colon epithelial cells reported by Smillie et al.31. The data demonstrate that LRRC8A was predominantly expressed in enterocytes, as well as in goblet cells (Fig. 4A, B). In line with our analysis of published GEO data, LRRC8A and LRRC8D were the primary subunits of VRAC in human IECs (Fig. 4B). Besides, the expression of LRRC8A and LRRC8D in enterocytes was increased in colitis patients compared to healthy donors (Fig. 4C). We also induced DSS colitis in Lrrc8d−/− mice to assess the role of LRRC8D in intestinal inflammation. Compared to controls, Lrrc8d−/− mice exhibited significantly worsened colitis symptoms (Fig. S4A–D). This suggests that while LRRC8A serves as the essential subunit of IEC VRAC, LRRC8D may act as another subunit critical for IEC VRAC functions. Notably, compared to heteromers containing LRRC8A combined with LRRC8C or LRRC8E, LRRC8A/8D-containing VRAC exhibits significantly higher permeability to large organic anions or uncharged osmolytes32,33. This unique biophysical property underscores the importance of LRRC8A/8D heteromers in mediating organic osmolytes transport and maintaining IEC homeostasis, positioning them as critical regulators of IEC physiology. However, Lrrc8d−/− mice exhibited increased consumption of DSS-containing water, although the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. S4E). This observation may reflect the essential role of VRAC in renal function34. We therefore focused on LRRC8A’s role in regulating IEC function in the present study. In WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice post-DSS challenge, the expression of mature enterocyte markers (Slc26a3, Alpi) was significantly decreased in colons isolated from Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 4D). In contrast, there were no notable expression changes in markers associated with stem cells (Lgr5, Ephb3), goblet cells (Muc2, Tff3), tuft cells (Dclk1, Trpm5), or enteroendocrine cells (Chga), supported by qPCR and bulk RNA-seq data (Fig. S5A, B). We further investigated the impact of epithelial VRAC on intestinal proliferation and turnover by measuring crypt Ki67 expression and tracking 12 h and 24 h 5-Ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU)+ labeling under homeostatic conditions. The number of Ki67+ cells in the crypts, as well as epithelial turnover rate, were compared between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S5C–F), suggesting that epithelial LRRC8A deficiency does not affect intestinal stemness or general differentiation, but specifically impairs the maturation and function of enterocytes.

We also generated LRRC8A-knockout Caco-2 cells (Caco-2ΔLRRC8A) and verified loss of VRAC function by electrophysiology (Fig. S6A, B). Swelling-activated currents displayed the characteristic voltage-dependent inactivation of VRAC at positive potentials, with tail currents upon repolarization to −80 mV reflecting recovery from inactivation. Loss of LRRC8A led to a marked reduction in TEER (Fig. S6C). In parallel, ZO-1 staining revealed increased junctional tortuosity and reduced signal intensity, indicative of tight-junction disruption (Fig. S6D). Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A partially rescued these barrier defects (Fig. S6E, F).

Along the colonic crypt–surface axis, enterocytes (clusters C1–C5) exhibit a spatially organized zonation program characterized by antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion and metal-ion handling at the crypt base, followed by progressive acquisition of metabolic and absorptive functions toward the luminal surface (Fig. 4E)11,35. Given the loss of IEC VRAC, specifically decreased enterocyte markers, we were prompted to explore the impact of VRAC on enterocyte zonation following DSS exposure, using enterocyte zonation genesets derived from the Moor et al.11 dataset. Our results indicated that the absence of IEC VRAC disrupts enterocyte zonation, causing a shift away from middle-top zone enterocytes toward a bottom-associated program characterized by elevated expression of AMP and metal-ion transporters (Fig. 4E, F).

To mimic the regenerative capacity of intestinal tissue and its ability to restore homeostasis following damage in vitro36, organoids were derived from the small intestine of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice. The surface area measurements and budding structure counts revealed no significant differences between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids samples, indicating that the proliferation or complexity of organoids was unaltered upon loss of VRAC in IECs (Fig. S7A, B). Immunofluorescence analysis of organoids for lineage-specific markers revealed a significant reduction in the enterocyte marker Alpi in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids compared to WT controls, whereas expression of the stem cell marker Lgr5 and goblet cell marker Muc2 remained comparable between genotypes (Fig. 4G). Overexpression of LRRC8A in organoids suppressed Alpi expression, consistent with the reduction of VRAC currents caused by LRRC8A overexpression in WT cells15. Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids restored Alpi expression, as shown by immunofluorescence and qPCR (Fig. 4H). These results indicate that while IEC VRAC is not essential for stemness, proliferation, or lineage allocation in intestinal organoids, it plays a specific role in promoting enterocyte differentiation and functional identity.

In addition, scRNA-seq was conducted using colonic epithelial cells pooled from 2 pairs of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice at 8 weeks of age. We profiled 2787 Lrrc8afl/fl cells and 4461 Lrrc8aΔIEC cells. Based on gene expression profiles, the cells were clustered into 10 distinct clusters (Clusters 1–10), which were categorized into six major cell populations.

reviewer_comments.reviewer_2:
In this study the authors investigate the role of a volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) in intestinal epithelium. They
cleary demonstrate that knock-out of subunits of this channel abolish (as it should) volume-activated anion currents. KO mice
with an intestinal-specific knock-out of the LRRC8A subunit seemed to have a normal physiology, but were much more
sensitive to inflammatory damage in classical IBD models. Changes in the expression of genes involved in retinoic acid
metabolism and beneficial effects of retinoic acid supplementation support the idea that this metabolite may play a central
role in the changes observed.
While this key message is clearly supported by the (quite large) number of different methodological approaches, there
remain some points to be clarified/rewritten to increase the impact of the paper.
In detail:
- p.23, line 666: Why did the hypotonic solution contain CsCl, whereas the isotonic solution contained KCl? With 140 mM
CsCl in the pipette, I would not assume that you need in addition an extracellular K+ channel blocker.
- Fig. S2: What was the reversal current of the swelling-induced current? It cannot be recognized from your ramp experiment.
The reversal potential would give you some hint about the selectivity of the conductance. In addition, the tail currents at the
end of your voltage-ramp should be discussed.
- Figure 3: Main components determining the permeability of the tight junctions are claudins. Did you observe any changes
in the claudin expression pattern?
- p.12, line 343: I do not think that the conclusion "... crucial role of gut microbiota in the protective role of VRAC..." is correct.
In all classical IBD models, you need gut microbiota to induce a colitis.
- Fig. 4E: You show here on the left enterocyte distribution from crypt to villus in the SMALL intestine (and refer to the paper
from Moor et al., working with proximal jejunum). However, the legend describes that in the right part of Fig. 4E your data
were collected from colon. There are no villi in the colon, there are only crypts and surface epithelium and transporters
expressed strongly differ between small and large intestine. In the whole manuscript, you must indicate whether your data
refer to small or large intestine.
reviewer_comments.reviewer_3:
Yi and colleagues report in their manuscript # NCOMMS-25-28940 that knocking out the essential volume-regulated 30
anion channel (VRAC) unit LRRC8A in epithelial cells of mice aggravates colitis and colitis-associated cancer. The
exacerbated colitis phenotype in these mice is associated with a disturbed enterocyte maturation and an altered gut
microbiota. Retinoid acid supplementation or lactobacillus administration partially reversed the observed phenotype in these
mice.
Major points
To better understand the role of VRAC in immunomodulatory metabolite transport, the authors should quantify extracellular
levels of known VRAC-exported metabolites such as cGAMP, itaconate, and glutamate. These measurements should be
conducted in conditioned media from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids or colon explants, both under basal conditions and
after DSS exposure, as well as in serum and fecal samples from DSS-treated WT and knockout mice. If VRAC facilitates the
export of anti-inflammatory metabolites, such as itaconate, its absence may cause intracellular retention, thereby
exacerbating inflammation. To functionally validate this mechanism, treating Lrrc8aΔIEC mice with exogenous itaconate or
cGAMP could be used to assess whether the inflammatory phenotype can be rescued.
To further substantiate the link between VRAC and epithelial-immune crosstalk, co-culture experiments should be performed
using WT or Lrrc8aΔIEC intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) with bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs), in the presence
or absence of DSS. The impact on immune modulation can be assessed by evaluating macrophage polarization (e.g., M1
vs. M2 markers) and cytokine secretion profiles. Additionally, neutrophil chemotaxis assays should be conducted to
determine whether supernatants from Lrrc8aΔIEC IECs enhance neutrophil migration, potentially contributing to the
heightened immune infiltration observed in vivo.
The authors should also investigate whether VRAC upregulation is protective in human IBD. This could be achieved by
performing immunohistochemical (IHC) staining for LRRC8A in colonic biopsies from IBD patients and correlating
expression levels with disease severity, tight junction integrity (e.g., ZO-1), and epithelial apoptosis (e.g., TUNEL staining).
To determine whether barrier loss in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice is linked to osmotic imbalance, transepithelial electrical resistance
(TEER) should be measured in WT and knockout colonoids under both isotonic and hypotonic conditions. A rescue
experiment using hypertonic media could help clarify whether restoring osmotic balance ameliorates tight junction disruption
and improves barrier integrity.
The observation that VRAC loss leads to increased tumor burden despite elevated epithelial apoptosis raises an important
mechanistic question. How can the authors explain these observations?
To explore the mechanistic link between VRAC and enterocyte maturation, rescue experiments should be performed using
Lrrc8aΔIEC IEC organoids. Specifically, re-expression of LRRC8A and LRRC8D via lentiviral transduction could help
determine whether the expression of mature enterocyte markers, such as Alpi and Slc26a3, can be restored. Additionally,
measuring the transport of organic osmolytes, such as taurine uptake, would provide a functional readout for enterocyte
maturation and VRAC activity.
To investigate VRAC-dependent zonation mechanisms, spatial transcriptomics could be applied to colon sections from WT
and Lrrc8aΔIEC IEC mice to map changes in epithelial zonation with high spatial resolution. Complementary experiments
using intestinal organoids treated with modulators of the Wnt and BMP pathways could reveal whether VRAC deficiency
alters responsiveness to these critical developmental gradients.
To assess the functional consequences of disrupted epithelial zonation, nutrient absorption capacity should be quantified by
measuring glucose and fatty acid uptake in Lrrc8aΔIEC enteroids. These findings can be further validated using Ussing
chamber assays on WT versus knockout colon explants. Metabolomic profiling of luminal contents via LC-MS could then be
used to correlate epithelial functional impairments with alterations in intestinal metabolic output.
The authors show impaired RA synthesis based on reduced expression of biosynthetic enzymes and RA-responsive genes.
However, direct quantification of RA levels in IECs and colon tissues from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mic using LC-MS or ELISA
would provide crucial biochemical validation.
To confirm that the observed defects in RA metabolism are epithelial-intrinsic, organoid cultures from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC
mice should be treated with retinol, and the capacity to generate RA (via ALDH activity or RA levels) should be compared in
vitro.
The authors should assess RAR/RXR transcriptional activity directly (e.g., using RA response element–luciferase reporters)
in WT and VRAC-deficient IECs ± atRA to demonstrate the functional consequences of impaired RA signaling.
While the authors demonstrate reduced IL-17A/IL-22 production, they should investigate whether this defect is rescued by
conditioned media from atRA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids, thereby supporting an epithelial-immune signaling axis.
The role of the microbiota would be more rigorously validated by transferring fecal microbiota from WT or Lrrc8aΔIEC mice
into germ-free recipients and assessing the severity of colitis after DSS treatment. This would test whether the microbiota
alone is sufficient to transfer susceptibility or protection.
To isolate the impact of RA-modified microbiota, fecal transplants from RA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC mice should be tested for
their ability to mitigate DSS-induced colitis when transplanted into antibiotic-pretreated WT or KO hosts.
The rescue effects of L. murinus and L. reuteri should be compared
mechanistically. For instance, do both strains restore ALDH activity, suppress AMP expression, and modulate immune responses in a similar manner? Do they influence RA
levels directly or via a secondary mechanism (e.g., bile acid modulation, SCFA)?
Minor points
Specify which IBD subtypes (UC, CD, or both) were analyzed in Fig. S1.

We sincerely thank all the Reviewers for their insightful and constructive comments.
As detailed in the point-by-point responses below, we have performed new experiments
to address the specific concerns raised by each Reviewer. We believe that these
additional data have substantially strengthened the manuscript. All newly generated
results have been incorporated into the revised manuscript.

isotonic solution contained KCl? With 140 mM CsCl in the pipette, I would not
assume that you need in addition an extracellular K+ channel blocker.
Response: We thank the Reviewer for this thoughtful comment. We agree that the use
of a CsCl-based pipette solution is sufficient to block the major potassium currents
activated under hypotonic conditions. The additional replacement of extracellular KCl
with CsCl was intended to further eliminate any potential residual contribution of
potassium currents during VRAC recordings. Similar intra- and extracellular CsCl-
based solutions have been used in previous publications 1,2.
2. - Fig. S2: What was the reversal current of the swelling-induced current? It
cannot be recognized from your ramp experiment. The reversal potential would
give you some hint about the selectivity of the conductance. In addition, the tail

Response: The reversal potential of the swelling-induced current was approximately -
6.56 mV (Fig. S2A), which is consistent with our previous studies2,3 and also confirms
that the current is predominantly mediated by Cl⁻ ions.
Time- and voltage-dependent inactivation at membrane potentials above +40 mV
is a characteristic electrophysiological feature of VRAC 4. Recovery from inactivation
is facilitated by negative membrane potentials, and the tail currents observed at –80 mV
reflect the recovery from inactivation. Similar tail-current behaviors have been reported
in multiple electrophysiological studies of VRAC 5,6. A brief explanation of the tail
currents has been incorporated into the revised manuscript.

the text has been revised to: “…these findings demonstrate that the heightened colitis

in the SMALL intestine (and refer to the paper from Moor et al., working with

Response: We thank the Reviewer for this comment. Although the small intestine and
colon differ in anatomy, they share a broadly conserved epithelial maturation gradient
that progresses from the crypt base toward the luminal surface. For example, Lorenzo-

small intestine, to classify bottom, middle, and top colonocytes in ex vivo “mini-colon”
cultures, demonstrating that these small-intestine zonation modules can reliably
annotate spatial differentiation states in the colon 7,8. Besides, Niec and colleagues also

maturation program. Using the SpaceFold framework, they reconstructed the epithelial
differentiation continuum for the small-intestinal crypt–villus axis and the colonic
crypt–surface axis within a unified pseudo-space. Their analysis indicated that small-
intestine zonation markers reflect conserved maturation patterns across the intestinal
epithelium 9. Collectively, these studies provide a well-established basis for applying
small-intestine zonation signatures to interpret colonic epithelial differentiation. In
accordance with the Reviewer’s suggestion, we have clarified this in the revised
manuscript and have corrected our terminology from “crypt–villus” to “crypt–axis”
when referring to colonic data.

different stages of inflammation-driven carcinogenesis. In our study, epithelial
apoptosis increases during acute DSS-induced injury as a downstream consequence of
severe mucosal damage. In contrast, under chronic or repetitive inflammatory
conditions, impaired epithelial regeneration and dysregulated repair create a
microenvironment that promotes the expansion and survival of transformed cells,

ultimately resulting in increased tumor burden. This progression is well supported by
previous reviews 16,17. Consistent with this framework, several experimental models
show that increased apoptosis during acute injury can coexist with enhanced
tumorigenesis during chronic inflammation. For example, cGAS-deficient mice exhibit

elevated proliferation within neoplastic lesions in the AOM-DSS model—illustrating
how impaired regeneration, rather than reduced apoptosis, governs tumor progression
10. Together, these findings support the concept that elevated apoptosis in the acute

components of inflammation-associated carcinogenesis.

You are an expert peer reviewer for Nature Communications, one of the world's leading multidisciplinary journals.

Read the following paper carefully and write a thorough, technically rigorous peer review. Identify the most important scientific concerns regarding: methodology, statistical analysis, data quality, claims vs. evidence, reproducibility, and clarity. Organise your review with clear sections.

## Abstract

Enterocytes mediate both nutrient absorption and antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion while constantly exposed to osmotic fluctuations. However, the role of volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC), a key osmo-sensitive ion channel, in enterocytes and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains unclear. Here, we show that intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific knockout of LRRC8A, the essential VRAC subunit, exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer. VRAC deficiency specifically disrupts enterocyte maturation and zonation, expanding AMP-producing enterocytes while reducing enterocytes responsible for nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism emerges as the most affected nutrient pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, with reduced Adh1, Aldh1a2 expression and aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. Supplementation with retinoic acid reversed inflammation caused by VRAC deficiency. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, while administration of Lactobacillus species effectively restored microbial balance and alleviated inflammation. This study delineates the role of VRAC in balancing nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes to safeguard gut homeostasis.

---

## Introduction

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic, relapsing disorder of the gastrointestinal tract and represents key risk factors for inflammation-associated colorectal cancer (CAC)1,2. Although the precise pathogenesis of IBD remains unclear, multiple factors have been implicated, including dysregulated immune responses, alterations in the gut microbiota, genetic predisposition, and environmental triggers.

Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs)—comprising stem cells, enterocytes, goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells, Paneth cells, and tuft cells—form a physical and functional barrier that not only separates luminal contents from the underlying mucosa but also regulates nutrient absorption and barrier integrity3. A growing body of evidence highlights the critical role of intestinal epithelial dysfunction in the initiation and progression of IBD, serving as a key interface that links luminal insults to aberrant immune activation and chronic inflammation4–6. Dysfunction in IEC differentiation, IEC-microbe interactions, or IEC-immune crosstalk plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of IBD or colorectal cancer7,8.

Among different types of IECs, enterocytes, which constitute approximately 90% of IECs, are the most prominent type and are responsible for nutrient and water absorption, and antimicrobial defense9,10. Importantly, enterocytes in both the small intestine and colon exhibit a spatially organized transcriptional and functional zonation pattern along the crypt–surface axis11–14. At the crypt base, enterocytes predominantly express genes involved in host defense, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and metal-ion transporters. As cells migrate upward, mid-zone enterocytes specialize in amino acid, vitamin, and carbohydrate absorption, while surface-located enterocytes are primarily responsible for lipid uptake11,12. Although nutrient malabsorption has been closely linked to the development and progression of IBD, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate enterocyte function in nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense—especially under inflammatory stress—remain poorly defined.

Mammalian cells need to regulate their volume by transporting ions and small organic osmolytes via ion channels and transporters to counteract osmotic swelling or shrinkage13,14. The volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) plays a pivotal role in restoring normal cell volume by mediating the efflux of chloride in response to cellular swelling14. VRAC is a heteromeric channel composed of subunits from the LRRC8 protein family (LRRC8A-E), with LRRC8A (also named SWELL1) being essential and required to heteromerize with at least one other subunit (LRRC8B–E) to form a functional channel15,16. In addition to transporting Cl−, VRAC is capable of transporting a wide variety of substances, including inositol, taurine, amino acids, and immune metabolites17–21. Notably, the specific heteromeric composition of VRAC subunits determines the channel’s distinct biophysical properties and physiological roles22,23. Serving as the largest barrier surface in the body, IECs are constantly exposed to significant osmolarity alterations caused by dietary intake, digestion, and various pathophysiological conditions24,25. However, little is known about the role of VRAC in regulating IEC function and its involvement in intestinal inflammation. In this study, we systematically investigated VRAC function in IECs using a combination of IEC-specific Lrrc8a conditional knockout mice and multiple inflammation models, including dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)- and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced colitis, as well as the azoxymethane (AOM)/DSS-induced inflammation-associated cancer model. We reveal that epithelial VRAC plays a critical role in preserving intestinal homeostasis under inflammatory conditions. Furthermore, deletion of Lrrc8d, encoding another key subunit of VRAC, also aggravated colitis, underscoring the functional importance of LRRC8A/8D-containing VRAC complexes in IECs. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that VRAC is specifically required for enterocyte maturation and zonation, as shown by scRNA-seq and organoid analyses. VRAC deficiency results in enterocyte reprogramming toward antimicrobial defense at the expense of nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism was the most impaired nutrient absorption pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, and its supplementation alleviated inflammation. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, notably reducing Lactobacillus species, while Lactobacillus administration mitigated inflammation caused by IEC VRAC loss. Collectively, our findings identify VRAC as a critical rheostat that coordinates nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes, thereby maintaining intestinal homeostasis during inflammation.

---

## Results

Intestinal VRAC loss exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer
To investigate the potential role of VRAC in IEC homeostasis and intestinal inflammation, we analyzed the expression levels of VRAC subunits in healthy individuals and IBD patients using published RNA-seq data from the GEO database. The data demonstrate that the expression of LRRC8A, the essential subunit of VRAC, was increased in the colon of IBD patients compared to healthy donors (Fig. S1A, B). LRRC8D, another key VRAC subunit, also exhibited high expression relative to other VRAC components, which indicates a potential link between VRAC and the development of IBD. Besides, immunohistochemistry showed slightly enhanced epithelial LRRC8A staining in CD biopsies, and this was accompanied by a modest increase in overall LRRC8A protein levels (Fig. S1C, D).

To determine the effects of VRAC in IECs and IBD, we generated IEC-specific Lrrc8a-knockout mice by crossing Lrrc8afl/fl mice with Villin1 (Vil1)-Cre transgenic mice26. These mice were hereinafter referred to as Lrrc8aΔIEC mice, whereas littermate Lrrc8afl/fl mice were used as WT controls (Fig. S2A). The loss of Lrrc8a in IECs of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was validated by qPCR and Western blot (Fig. S2B, C). The body weight, water intake, and spleen weight were similar between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2D–F). Besides, the deletion of LRRC8A in IECs had no significant effect on fecal weight or water content (Fig. S2G). Histology and tight-junction markers of the colon and distal ileum also showed no overt abnormalities between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2H–K). These suggest VRAC in IECs is dispensable for the functionality of intestinal epithelia in the steady state. To elucidate the potential role of VRAC in IECs upon inflammatory stress, WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice were then subjected to DSS-induced colitis27. Of note, greater body weight loss and higher disease activity index (DAI) upon challenge with 1.5% or 2.5% DSS was observed in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 1A, B). The colon length of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was much shorter than that of WT mice upon DSS challenge, indicating more severe inflammatory damage (Fig. 1C). Moreover, the lethality in the Lrrc8aΔIEC mice subjected to 3% DSS was significantly increased (Fig. 1D). Furthermore, Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited heightened epithelial erosion and inflammation, along with a pronounced reduction in mucus-secreting goblet cells after DSS treatment (Fig. 1E, F). A growing body of evidence highlights the critical role of intestinal epithelial dysfunction in the initiation and progression of IBD, serving as a key interface that links luminal insults to aberrant immune activation and chronic inflammation4–6. Dysfunction in IEC differentiation, IEC-microbe interactions, or IEC-immune crosstalk plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of IBD or colorectal cancer7,8.

Among different types of IECs, enterocytes, which constitute approximately 90% of IECs, are the most prominent type and are responsible for nutrient and water absorption, and antimicrobial defense9,10. Although nutrient malabsorption has been closely linked to the development and progression of IBD, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate enterocyte function in nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense—especially under inflammatory stress—remain poorly defined.

Mammalian cells need to regulate their volume by transporting ions and small organic osmolytes via ion channels and transporters to counteract osmotic swelling or shrinkage13,14. We further investigated the impact of epithelial VRAC on intestinal proliferation and turnover by measuring crypt Ki67 expression and tracking 12 h and 24 h 5-Ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU)+ labeling under homeostatic conditions. The number of Ki67+ cells in the crypts, as well as epithelial turnover rate, were compared between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S5C–F), suggesting that epithelial LRRC8A deficiency does not affect intestinal stemness or general differentiation, but specifically impairs the maturation and function of enterocytes.

We also generated LRRC8A-knockout Caco-2 cells (Caco-2ΔLRRC8A) and verified loss of VRAC function by electrophysiology (Fig. S6A, B). Swelling-activated currents displayed the characteristic voltage-dependent inactivation of VRAC at positive potentials, with tail currents upon repolarization to −80 mV reflecting recovery from inactivation. Loss of LRRC8A led to a marked reduction in TEER (Fig. S6C). In parallel, ZO-1 staining revealed increased junctional tortuosity and reduced signal intensity, indicative of tight-junction disruption (Fig. S6D). Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A partially rescued these barrier defects (Fig. S6E, F).

Along the colonic crypt–surface axis, enterocytes (clusters C1–C5) exhibit a spatially organized zonation program characterized by antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion and metal-ion handling at the crypt base, followed by progressive acquisition of metabolic and absorptive functions toward the luminal surface (Fig. 4E)11,35. Given the loss of IEC VRAC, specifically decreased enterocyte markers, we were prompted to explore the impact of VRAC on enterocyte zonation following DSS exposure, using enterocyte zonation genesets derived from the Moor et al.11 dataset. Our results indicated that the absence of IEC VRAC disrupts enterocyte zonation, causing a shift away from middle-top zone enterocytes toward a bottom-associated program characterized by elevated expression of AMP and metal-ion transporters (Fig. 4E, F).

To mimic the regenerative capacity of intestinal tissue and its ability to restore homeostasis following damage in vitro36, organoids were derived from the small intestine of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice. The surface area measurements and budding structure counts revealed no significant differences between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids samples, indicating that the proliferation or complexity of organoids was unaltered upon loss of VRAC in IECs (Fig. S7A, B). Immunofluorescence analysis of organoids for lineage-specific markers revealed a significant reduction in the enterocyte marker Alpi in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids compared to WT controls, whereas expression of the stem cell marker Lgr5 and goblet cell marker Muc2 remained comparable between genotypes (Fig. 4G). Overexpression of LRRC8A in organoids suppressed Alpi expression, consistent with the reduction of VRAC currents caused by LRRC8A overexpression in WT cells15. Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids restored Alpi expression, as shown by immunofluorescence and qPCR (Fig. 4H). These results indicate that while IEC VRAC is not essential for stemness, proliferation, or lineage allocation in intestinal organoids, it plays a specific role in promoting enterocyte differentiation and functional identity.

In addition, scRNA-seq was conducted using colonic epithelial cells pooled from 2 pairs of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice at 8 weeks of age. We profiled 2787 Lrrc8afl/fl cells and 4461 Lrrc8aΔIEC cells. Based on gene expression profiles, the cells were clustered into 10 distinct clusters (Clusters 1–10), which were categorized into six major cell populations.

responsiveness to these critical developmental gradients.
Response: Given the established roles of Wnt/BMP signaling in orchestrating intestinal
epithelial lineage differentiation18,19, we systematically analyzed transcriptomic
alterations in these pathways. RT-qPCR analysis of canonical Wnt signaling markers
(Ascl2 and Axin2) in colon tissues from DSS-treated mice and in vitro organoid cultures
revealed no significant differences between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC groups (revised Fig.
S7I and Fig. 4L). Meanwhile, β-catenin immunostaining in organoids demonstrated
comparable levels of both total and nuclear-localized β-catenin across both genotypes
(revised Fig. S7J). In contrast, BMP2, one of the major BMP ligands in the intestine,
was significantly reduced in Lrrc8aΔIEC colon tissues and organoids (revised Fig. S7I
8
and Fig. 4L). Moreover, exogenous BMP2 supplementation substantially restored Alpi
expression in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids (revised Fig. 4M). These findings indicate that
VRAC regulates intestinal epithelial zonation through a BMP2-dependent mechanism.
8. To assess the functional consequences of disrupted epithelial zonation,
nutrient absorption capacity should be quantified by measuring glucose and
fatty acid uptake in Lrrc8aΔIEC enteroids. These findings can be further
validated using Ussing chamber assays on WT versus knockout colon explants.
Metabolomic profiling of luminal contents via LC-MS could then be used to
correlate epithelial functional impairments with alterations in intestinal
metabolic output.
Response: To evaluate the functional consequences of disrupted epithelial zonation, we
performed glucose and lipid uptake assays in WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids. The data
demonstrates that VRAC deficiency significantly impaired lipid absorption. The
glucose uptake was also reduced, the magnitude of inhibition was weaker compared
with the defect in lipid absorption (revised Fig. S7C, D). Together with our
transcriptomic and metabolomic data, these findings indicate that loss of epithelial
VRAC causes broad defects in enterocyte zonation and maturation, leading to
substantial impairment of nutrient-absorptive functions. Our data demonstrates that
impaired retinoic acid (RA) metabolism is a key factor contributing to the exacerbated
inflammation observed in the absence of epithelial VRAC. RA has been shown to
regulate enterocyte differentiation and modulate both T cell and ILC functions, thereby
shaping intestinal inflammatory responses20,21. Consistent with these roles, our in vivo
and in vitro experiments indicate that disrupted RA metabolism provides a mechanistic
explanation for the defective enterocyte zonation and compromised nutrient absorption
in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice.
9. The authors show impaired RA synthesis based on reduced expression of
biosynthetic enzymes and RA-responsive genes. However, direct quantification
of RA levels in IECs and colon tissues from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mic using LC-
MS or ELISA would provide crucial biochemical validation.
Response: RA levels in colonic tissue are physiologically very low, typically on the
order of ~10 pmol per gram of tissue, which makes their direct quantification
technically challenging22,23. During our study, we attempted to measure RA in colon
samples using LC-MS; however, the signal intensity was below the threshold required
to generate reliable peak identification. We also surveyed all available commercial kits
and found that no validated ELISA assays exist for RA detection in tissue samples.
Given these technical limitations, we assessed RA activity through established
indirect readouts. Measuring the expression of Aldh enzymes, the rate-limiting
regulators of RA synthesis, is widely used to surrogate measure for RA content24–26. In
addition, both in vivo and in vitro experiments demonstrated that atRA supplementation
restored the expression of RA-responsive genes and key differentiation markers. These
results confirm that RA signaling is indeed impaired in VRAC-deficient intestinal
epithelial cells, and that this pathway remains functionally responsive when exogenous
RA is provided.
9
10. To confirm that the observed defects in RA metabolism are epithelial-
intrinsic, organoid cultures from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice should be treated
with retinol, and the capacity to generate RA (via ALDH activity or RA levels)
should be compared in vitro.
Response: Retinol enhanced Alpi expression and ALDH activity in Lrrc8aΔIEC
organoids, although these effects were significantly attenuated compared to direct atRA
administration (revised Fig. S10E, F), suggesting impaired retinol uptake in the
absence of VRAC.
11. The authors should assess RAR/RXR transcriptional activity directly (e.g.,
using RA response element–luciferase reporters) in WT and VRAC-deficient
IECs ± atRA to demonstrate the functional consequences of impaired RA
signaling.
Response: We agree that direct assessment of RAR/RXR transcriptional activity using
RARE-luciferase reporters would provide valuable mechanistic insight. However, in
intestinal epithelial cell systems such as Caco-2 cells, reporter-based assays are difficult
to interpret due to consistently low transfection efficiency. Our organoid and in vivo
atRA supplementation studies demonstrate that epithelial VRAC is functionally
connected to RA signaling. atRA treatment effectively rescued Alpi expression, ALDH
activity, and other RA-responsive markers in VRAC-deficient models, demonstrating
that RA signaling impairment underlies the defects caused by VRAC loss. We therefore
consider these rescue experiments to provide a physiologically relevant readout of RA
pathway activity.
12. While the authors demonstrate reduced IL-17A/IL-22 production, they
should investigate whether this defect is rescued by conditioned media from
atRA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids, thereby supporting an epithelial-immune
signaling axis.
Response: As noted above and in our response to Comment #2, we consider organoid
supernatants unsuitable for directly stimulating immune cells. Organoid cultures often
release endotoxins and contain complex, incompletely defined components derived
from Matrigel, making it difficult to attribute immunological effects to specific
epithelial-derived factors. While organoid conditioned medium has influenced immune
cells like DCs and CTLs, direct evidence for its role in stimulating T and ILC cells to
secrete IL-17A/IL-22 is limited27. Accordingly, most high-quality studies rely on direct
immune cell–organoid co-culture rather than immune stimulation with organoid
supernatants. As mentioned earlier, we collected conditioned media from Caco-2WT and
Caco-2ΔLRRC8A cells and applied them to in vitro-differentiated splenic Th17 and ILC3
cultures. Our results showed that supernatants from Caco-2ΔLRRC8A cells markedly
reduced the proportions of IL-17A⁺ and IL-22⁺ Th17 and ILC3 cells (revised Fig. 6E,
F). These findings demonstrate that epithelial VRAC deficiency alters epithelial
metabolism that modulate innate lymphoid and T-cell effector functions, supporting a
critical epithelial-immune signaling axis disrupted by the epithelial loss of VRAC.
13. The role of the microbiota would be more rigorously validated by transferring
fecal microbiota from WT or Lrrc8aΔIEC mice into germ-free recipients and
10
assessing the severity of colitis after DSS treatment. This would test whether
the microbiota alone is sufficient to transfer susceptibility or protection.
Response: To further validate the role of the microbiota, we transferred fecal
microbiota collected from DSS-treated WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC donor mice into antibiotic-
pretreated recipient mice. Our results showed that recipients receiving microbiota from
DSS-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC donors developed markedly more severe colitis following DSS
challenge (revised Fig. 7E–H). These findings demonstrate that the dysbiotic
microbiota arising in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice under inflammatory condition is sufficient to
confer increased susceptibility to colitis.
14. To isolate the impact of RA-modified microbiota, fecal transplants from RA-
treated Lrrc8aΔIEC mice should be tested for their ability to mitigate DSS-
induced colitis when transplanted into antibiotic-pretreated WT or KO hosts.
Response: We appreciate the Reviewer’s thoughtful suggestion. However, DSS-
induced colitis is strictly microbiota-dependent. In our ABX-pretreated recipients, the
overall microbial load is greatly reduced, and under these conditions both WT and
Lrrc8aΔIEC mice develop little to no colitis, which is consistent with previous reports
(revised Fig. S12A–D). Similarly, RA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibit minimal disease
even without transfer. Therefore, transferring microbiota from RA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC
donors into antibiotic-pretreated recipients would not be informative, as both donor and
recipient conditions result in negligible disease, precluding a meaningful assessment of
microbiota-mediated protection.
15. The rescue effects of L. murinus and L. reuteri should be compared
mechanistically. For instance, do both strains restore ALDH activity, suppress
AMP expression, and modulate immune responses in a similar manner? Do
they influence RA levels directly or via a secondary mechanism (e.g., bile acid
modulation, SCFA)?
Response: We performed additional experiments to more directly compare the effects
of different Lactobacillus strains. Our new data show that L. reuteri supplementation,
similar to L. murinus, restored epithelial ALDH activity, normalized tissue AMP
expression, and recovered IL-17A⁺ and IL-22⁺ lymphocyte populations in the lamina
propria of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (revised Fig. 8F–H; revised Fig. S12J–L). In addition,
updated metabolomic analyses revealed alterations in several bile acid species under
epithelial VRAC deficiency (revised Fig. S7G, H). We consider these bile acid
perturbations to be a consequence of disrupted epithelial zonation under IEC VRAC
deficiency. Although we cannot exclude the possibility that VRAC may directly
influence the transport of certain bile acids or related lipid metabolites, clarifying
whether VRAC contributes through direct permeability or indirect secondary
mechanisms will require future investigation.
Together, these new findings support a coherent mechanistic model in which
Lactobacillus supplementation enhances RA metabolism and restores enterocyte
zonation, thereby ameliorating epithelial–immune dysregulation in IEC VRAC-
deficient mice.

Response: We thank the Reviewer for this comment. We have now specified the IBD

## Paper

## Abstract

Enterocytes mediate both nutrient absorption and antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion while constantly exposed to osmotic fluctuations. However, the role of volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC), a key osmo-sensitive ion channel, in enterocytes and inflammatory bowel disease (IBD) remains unclear. Here, we show that intestinal epithelial cell (IEC)-specific knockout of LRRC8A, the essential VRAC subunit, exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer. VRAC deficiency specifically disrupts enterocyte maturation and zonation, expanding AMP-producing enterocytes while reducing enterocytes responsible for nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism emerges as the most affected nutrient pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, with reduced Adh1, Aldh1a2 expression and aldehyde dehydrogenase activity. Supplementation with retinoic acid reversed inflammation caused by VRAC deficiency. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, while administration of Lactobacillus species effectively restored microbial balance and alleviated inflammation. This study delineates the role of VRAC in balancing nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes to safeguard gut homeostasis.

---

## Introduction

Inflammatory bowel disease (IBD), including Crohn’s disease (CD) and ulcerative colitis (UC), is a chronic, relapsing disorder of the gastrointestinal tract and represents key risk factors for inflammation-associated colorectal cancer (CAC)1,2. Although the precise pathogenesis of IBD remains unclear, multiple factors have been implicated, including dysregulated immune responses, alterations in the gut microbiota, genetic predisposition, and environmental triggers.

Intestinal epithelial cells (IECs)—comprising stem cells, enterocytes, goblet cells, enteroendocrine cells, Paneth cells, and tuft cells—form a physical and functional barrier that not only separates luminal contents from the underlying mucosa but also regulates nutrient absorption and barrier integrity3. A growing body of evidence highlights the critical role of intestinal epithelial dysfunction in the initiation and progression of IBD, serving as a key interface that links luminal insults to aberrant immune activation and chronic inflammation4–6. Dysfunction in IEC differentiation, IEC-microbe interactions, or IEC-immune crosstalk plays a critical role in the pathogenesis of IBD or colorectal cancer7,8.

Among different types of IECs, enterocytes, which constitute approximately 90% of IECs, are the most prominent type and are responsible for nutrient and water absorption, and antimicrobial defense9,10. Importantly, enterocytes in both the small intestine and colon exhibit a spatially organized transcriptional and functional zonation pattern along the crypt–surface axis11–14. At the crypt base, enterocytes predominantly express genes involved in host defense, such as antimicrobial peptides (AMPs) and metal-ion transporters. As cells migrate upward, mid-zone enterocytes specialize in amino acid, vitamin, and carbohydrate absorption, while surface-located enterocytes are primarily responsible for lipid uptake11,12. Although nutrient malabsorption has been closely linked to the development and progression of IBD, the molecular mechanisms that coordinate enterocyte function in nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense—especially under inflammatory stress—remain poorly defined.

Mammalian cells need to regulate their volume by transporting ions and small organic osmolytes via ion channels and transporters to counteract osmotic swelling or shrinkage13,14. The volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) plays a pivotal role in restoring normal cell volume by mediating the efflux of chloride in response to cellular swelling14. VRAC is a heteromeric channel composed of subunits from the LRRC8 protein family (LRRC8A-E), with LRRC8A (also named SWELL1) being essential and required to heteromerize with at least one other subunit (LRRC8B–E) to form a functional channel15,16. In addition to transporting Cl−, VRAC is capable of transporting a wide variety of substances, including inositol, taurine, amino acids, and immune metabolites17–21. Notably, the specific heteromeric composition of VRAC subunits determines the channel’s distinct biophysical properties and physiological roles22,23. Serving as the largest barrier surface in the body, IECs are constantly exposed to significant osmolarity alterations caused by dietary intake, digestion, and various pathophysiological conditions24,25. However, little is known about the role of VRAC in regulating IEC function and its involvement in intestinal inflammation. In this study, we systematically investigated VRAC function in IECs using a combination of IEC-specific Lrrc8a conditional knockout mice and multiple inflammation models, including dextran sodium sulfate (DSS)- and 2,4,6-trinitrobenzenesulfonic acid (TNBS)-induced colitis, as well as the azoxymethane (AOM)/DSS-induced inflammation-associated cancer model. We reveal that epithelial VRAC plays a critical role in preserving intestinal homeostasis under inflammatory conditions. Furthermore, deletion of Lrrc8d, encoding another key subunit of VRAC, also aggravated colitis, underscoring the functional importance of LRRC8A/8D-containing VRAC complexes in IECs. Mechanistically, we demonstrate that VRAC is specifically required for enterocyte maturation and zonation, as shown by scRNA-seq and organoid analyses. VRAC deficiency results in enterocyte reprogramming toward antimicrobial defense at the expense of nutrient absorption. Retinoic acid metabolism was the most impaired nutrient absorption pathway in VRAC-deficient IECs, and its supplementation alleviated inflammation. Conversely, VRAC deficiency induced gut microbiota dysbiosis, notably reducing Lactobacillus species, while Lactobacillus administration mitigated inflammation caused by IEC VRAC loss. Collectively, our findings identify VRAC as a critical rheostat that coordinates nutrient absorption and antimicrobial defense in enterocytes, thereby maintaining intestinal homeostasis during inflammation.

---

## Results

Intestinal VRAC loss exacerbates colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer
To investigate the potential role of VRAC in IEC homeostasis and intestinal inflammation, we analyzed the expression levels of VRAC subunits in healthy individuals and IBD patients using published RNA-seq data from the GEO database. The data demonstrate that the expression of LRRC8A, the essential subunit of VRAC, was increased in the colon of IBD patients compared to healthy donors (Fig. S1A, B). LRRC8D, another key VRAC subunit, also exhibited high expression relative to other VRAC components, which indicates a potential link between VRAC and the development of IBD. Besides, immunohistochemistry showed slightly enhanced epithelial LRRC8A staining in CD biopsies, and this was accompanied by a modest increase in overall LRRC8A protein levels (Fig. S1C, D).

To determine the effects of VRAC in IECs and IBD, we generated IEC-specific Lrrc8a-knockout mice by crossing Lrrc8afl/fl mice with Villin1 (Vil1)-Cre transgenic mice26. These mice were hereinafter referred to as Lrrc8aΔIEC mice, whereas littermate Lrrc8afl/fl mice were used as WT controls (Fig. S2A). The loss of Lrrc8a in IECs of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was validated by qPCR and Western blot (Fig. S2B, C). The body weight, water intake, and spleen weight were similar between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2D–F). Besides, the deletion of LRRC8A in IECs had no significant effect on fecal weight or water content (Fig. S2G). Histology and tight-junction markers of the colon and distal ileum also showed no overt abnormalities between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S2H–K). These suggest VRAC in IECs is dispensable for the functionality of intestinal epithelia in the steady state. To elucidate the potential role of VRAC in IECs upon inflammatory stress, WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice were then subjected to DSS-induced colitis27. Of note, greater body weight loss and higher disease activity index (DAI) upon challenge with 1.5% or 2.5% DSS was observed in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice compared to WT mice (Fig. 1A, B). The colon length of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice was much shorter than that of WT mice upon DSS challenge, indicating more severe inflammatory damage (Fig. 1C). Moreover, the lethality in the Lrrc8aΔIEC mice subjected to 3% DSS was significantly increased (Fig. 1D). Furthermore, Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited heightened epithelial erosion and inflammation, along with a pronounced reduction in mucus-secreting goblet cells after DSS treatment (Fig. 1E, F). To further validate the role of VRAC in intestinal inflammation, we established a TNBS-induced colitis model, which closely mimics the immunepathology of CD. Lrrc8aΔIEC mice also exhibited reduced colon length and enhanced inflammation, together with greater body weight loss (Fig. S3). Taken together, these findings suggest that intestinal VRAC plays a vital protective role in the development and progression of colitis.

VRAC and cell volume regulation have been shown to transport specific immune metabolites such as cGAMP and itaconate, thereby playing key roles in both innate and adaptive immunity28,29. Thereby, Lrrc8afl/fl mice were also crossed with LysM-Cre mice or CD4-Cre mice, to achieve conditional ablation of Lrrc8a in myeloid cells (Lrrc8aΔLysM) or T cells (Lrrc8aΔCD4), respectively (Fig. S2A). However, the results demonstrate that mice lacking Lrrc8a in either myeloid cells or T cells exhibited comparable weight loss, DAI, colon shortening, and histopathological features compared to control littermates upon DSS challenge (Fig. 1G–L). These findings emphasize that it is intestinal epithelial VRAC, rather than immune cell-intrinsic VRAC, that plays a critical role in protecting against intestinal inflammation.

IBD is a well-established risk factor for the development of inflammation-associated colorectal cancer30. We further explored the role of intestinal VRAC in the development of inflammation-associated colorectal cancer by using AOM combined with low concentrations of DSS (1%), given that Lrrc8aΔIEC mice tended to succumb to DSS exposure. Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited significantly more body weight loss during DSS treatment (Fig. 2A). At day 80 post-AOM-DSS treatment, colons of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice developed a markedly increased tumor burden, including higher tumor numbers and larger tumor sizes (Fig. 2B–D). Histological analysis revealed a greater extent of inflammation and epithelial hyperplasia in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 2E–G). Taken together, our data demonstrate a crucial role of intestinal VRAC in protecting the intestine against inflammatory stimuli, including colitis and inflammation-associated colorectal cancer.

Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited enhanced inflammatory responses and intestinal epithelial damage
Next, we performed bulk RNA-seq analysis using colon RNAs from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice after DSS challenge. In Lrrc8aΔIEC mice, 110 genes were notably downregulated, while 355 genes were significantly upregulated (|log FC|>1; adjusted P<0.05) (Fig. 3A). Gene ontology (GO) analysis by Enrichr showed a significant upregulation associated with inflammatory response genes, neutrophil migration, and antimicrobial response. Whereas, genes involved in lipid transport and ion transport exhibited a noticeable reduction in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 3B). Inflammatory genes (e.g., Cxcl10, Il6) were significantly increased, as confirmed via qPCR, in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice subjected to DSS or AOM-DSS treatment (Fig. 3C, E). Besides, the expression levels of AMPs such as calprotectin subunits S100a8 and S100a9, were markedly elevated in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 3D). Moreover, increased apoptosis and reduced epithelial cell proliferation in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice were observed by enhanced staining for TUNEL along with decreased staining for the proliferation marker Ki67, demonstrating impaired intestinal healing (Fig. 3F). Thus, the loss of VRAC results in enhanced inflammatory and antimicrobial responses while decreasing ion and lipid transport under intestinal inflammatory stress.

Given the central role of intestinal barrier dysfunctions in intestinal inflammation, we examined whether IEC VRAC deficiency compromised the barrier integrity by analyzing the distribution or expression of tight-junction protein zonula occludens-1 (ZO-1), Occludin, and Claudin-2. Consistently, colons from Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibited notably disrupted tight junctions (Fig. 3G), suggesting a compromised mucosal barrier in Lrrc8aΔIEC mice. This was further confirmed by the elevated fluorescence in the serum of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice fed with FITC-labeled dextran (MW 4000), indicative of colonic leakage (Fig. 3H). The data reveal that VRAC in IECs is crucial for maintaining the intestinal barrier and provides significant protection against colitis and CAC.

Intestinal VRAC is specifically required for enterocyte maturation and zonation
To explore the underlying mechanism by which IEC VRAC protects against intestinal inflammation, we analyzed different VRAC subunits in IECs using single-cell RNA sequencing (scRNA-seq) data of human colon epithelial cells reported by Smillie et al.31. The data demonstrate that LRRC8A was predominantly expressed in enterocytes, as well as in goblet cells (Fig. 4A, B). In line with our analysis of published GEO data, LRRC8A and LRRC8D were the primary subunits of VRAC in human IECs (Fig. 4B). Besides, the expression of LRRC8A and LRRC8D in enterocytes was increased in colitis patients compared to healthy donors (Fig. 4C). We also induced DSS colitis in Lrrc8d−/− mice to assess the role of LRRC8D in intestinal inflammation. Compared to controls, Lrrc8d−/− mice exhibited significantly worsened colitis symptoms (Fig. S4A–D). This suggests that while LRRC8A serves as the essential subunit of IEC VRAC, LRRC8D may act as another subunit critical for IEC VRAC functions. Notably, compared to heteromers containing LRRC8A combined with LRRC8C or LRRC8E, LRRC8A/8D-containing VRAC exhibits significantly higher permeability to large organic anions or uncharged osmolytes32,33. This unique biophysical property underscores the importance of LRRC8A/8D heteromers in mediating organic osmolytes transport and maintaining IEC homeostasis, positioning them as critical regulators of IEC physiology. However, Lrrc8d−/− mice exhibited increased consumption of DSS-containing water, although the difference was not statistically significant (Fig. S4E). This observation may reflect the essential role of VRAC in renal function34. We therefore focused on LRRC8A’s role in regulating IEC function in the present study. In WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice post-DSS challenge, the expression of mature enterocyte markers (Slc26a3, Alpi) was significantly decreased in colons isolated from Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. 4D). In contrast, there were no notable expression changes in markers associated with stem cells (Lgr5, Ephb3), goblet cells (Muc2, Tff3), tuft cells (Dclk1, Trpm5), or enteroendocrine cells (Chga), supported by qPCR and bulk RNA-seq data (Fig. S5A, B). We further investigated the impact of epithelial VRAC on intestinal proliferation and turnover by measuring crypt Ki67 expression and tracking 12 h and 24 h 5-Ethynyl-2-deoxyuridine (EdU)+ labeling under homeostatic conditions. The number of Ki67+ cells in the crypts, as well as epithelial turnover rate, were compared between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (Fig. S5C–F), suggesting that epithelial LRRC8A deficiency does not affect intestinal stemness or general differentiation, but specifically impairs the maturation and function of enterocytes.

We also generated LRRC8A-knockout Caco-2 cells (Caco-2ΔLRRC8A) and verified loss of VRAC function by electrophysiology (Fig. S6A, B). Swelling-activated currents displayed the characteristic voltage-dependent inactivation of VRAC at positive potentials, with tail currents upon repolarization to −80 mV reflecting recovery from inactivation. Loss of LRRC8A led to a marked reduction in TEER (Fig. S6C). In parallel, ZO-1 staining revealed increased junctional tortuosity and reduced signal intensity, indicative of tight-junction disruption (Fig. S6D). Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A partially rescued these barrier defects (Fig. S6E, F).

Along the colonic crypt–surface axis, enterocytes (clusters C1–C5) exhibit a spatially organized zonation program characterized by antimicrobial peptide (AMP) secretion and metal-ion handling at the crypt base, followed by progressive acquisition of metabolic and absorptive functions toward the luminal surface (Fig. 4E)11,35. Given the loss of IEC VRAC, specifically decreased enterocyte markers, we were prompted to explore the impact of VRAC on enterocyte zonation following DSS exposure, using enterocyte zonation genesets derived from the Moor et al.11 dataset. Our results indicated that the absence of IEC VRAC disrupts enterocyte zonation, causing a shift away from middle-top zone enterocytes toward a bottom-associated program characterized by elevated expression of AMP and metal-ion transporters (Fig. 4E, F).

To mimic the regenerative capacity of intestinal tissue and its ability to restore homeostasis following damage in vitro36, organoids were derived from the small intestine of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice. The surface area measurements and budding structure counts revealed no significant differences between WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids samples, indicating that the proliferation or complexity of organoids was unaltered upon loss of VRAC in IECs (Fig. S7A, B). Immunofluorescence analysis of organoids for lineage-specific markers revealed a significant reduction in the enterocyte marker Alpi in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids compared to WT controls, whereas expression of the stem cell marker Lgr5 and goblet cell marker Muc2 remained comparable between genotypes (Fig. 4G). Overexpression of LRRC8A in organoids suppressed Alpi expression, consistent with the reduction of VRAC currents caused by LRRC8A overexpression in WT cells15. Notably, re-expression of LRRC8A in Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids restored Alpi expression, as shown by immunofluorescence and qPCR (Fig. 4H). These results indicate that while IEC VRAC is not essential for stemness, proliferation, or lineage allocation in intestinal organoids, it plays a specific role in promoting enterocyte differentiation and functional identity.

In addition, scRNA-seq was conducted using colonic epithelial cells pooled from 2 pairs of WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC mice at 8 weeks of age. We profiled 2787 Lrrc8afl/fl cells and 4461 Lrrc8aΔIEC cells. Based on gene expression profiles, the cells were clustered into 10 distinct clusters (Clusters 1–10), which were categorized into six major cell populations.

## Round 1 — Reviewer Comments

### Reviewer 2

In this study the authors investigate the role of a volume-regulated anion channel (VRAC) in intestinal epithelium. They
cleary demonstrate that knock-out of subunits of this channel abolish (as it should) volume-activated anion currents. KO mice
with an intestinal-specific knock-out of the LRRC8A subunit seemed to have a normal physiology, but were much more
sensitive to inflammatory damage in classical IBD models. Changes in the expression of genes involved in retinoic acid
metabolism and beneficial effects of retinoic acid supplementation support the idea that this metabolite may play a central
role in the changes observed.
While this key message is clearly supported by the (quite large) number of different methodological approaches, there
remain some points to be clarified/rewritten to increase the impact of the paper.
In detail:
- p.23, line 666: Why did the hypotonic solution contain CsCl, whereas the isotonic solution contained KCl? With 140 mM
CsCl in the pipette, I would not assume that you need in addition an extracellular K+ channel blocker.
- Fig. S2: What was the reversal current of the swelling-induced current? It cannot be recognized from your ramp experiment.
The reversal potential would give you some hint about the selectivity of the conductance. In addition, the tail currents at the
end of your voltage-ramp should be discussed.
- Figure 3: Main components determining the permeability of the tight junctions are claudins. Did you observe any changes
in the claudin expression pattern?
- p.12, line 343: I do not think that the conclusion "... crucial role of gut microbiota in the protective role of VRAC..." is correct.
In all classical IBD models, you need gut microbiota to induce a colitis.
- Fig. 4E: You show here on the left enterocyte distribution from crypt to villus in the SMALL intestine (and refer to the paper
from Moor et al., working with proximal jejunum). However, the legend describes that in the right part of Fig. 4E your data

### Reviewer 3

Yi and colleagues report in their manuscript # NCOMMS-25-28940 that knocking out the essential volume-regulated 30
anion channel (VRAC) unit LRRC8A in epithelial cells of mice aggravates colitis and colitis-associated cancer. The
exacerbated colitis phenotype in these mice is associated with a disturbed enterocyte maturation and an altered gut

Major points
To better understand the role of VRAC in immunomodulatory metabolite transport, the authors should quantify extracellular
levels of known VRAC-exported metabolites such as cGAMP, itaconate, and glutamate. These measurements should be
conducted in conditioned media from WT and Lrrc8aΔIEC organoids or colon explants, both under basal conditions and
after DSS exposure, as well as in serum and fecal samples from DSS-treated WT and knockout mice. If VRAC facilitates the
export of anti-inflammatory metabolites, such as itaconate, its absence may cause intracellular retention, thereby
exacerbating inflammation. To functionally validate this mechanism, treating Lrrc8aΔIEC mice with exogenous itaconate or
cGAMP could be used to assess whether the inflammatory phenotype can be rescued.
To further substantiate the link between VRAC and epithelial-immune crosstalk, co-culture experiments should be performed
using WT or Lrrc8aΔIEC intestinal epithelial cells (IECs) with bone marrow-derived macrophages (BMDMs), in the presence

induced colitis is strictly microbiota-dependent. In our ABX-pretreated recipients, the
overall microbial load is greatly reduced, and under these conditions both WT and
Lrrc8aΔIEC mice develop little to no colitis, which is consistent with previous reports
(revised Fig. S12A–D). Similarly, RA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC mice exhibit minimal disease
even without transfer. Therefore, transferring microbiota from RA-treated Lrrc8aΔIEC
donors into antibiotic-pretreated recipients would not be informative, as both donor and
recipient conditions result in negligible disease, precluding a meaningful assessment of
microbiota-mediated protection.
15. The rescue effects of L. murinus and L. reuteri should be compared
mechanistically. For instance, do both strains restore ALDH activity, suppress
AMP expression, and modulate immune responses in a similar manner? Do
they influence RA levels directly or via a secondary mechanism (e.g., bile acid
modulation, SCFA)?
Response: We performed additional experiments to more directly compare the effects
of different Lactobacillus strains. Our new data show that L. reuteri supplementation,
similar to L. murinus, restored epithelial ALDH activity, normalized tissue AMP
expression, and recovered IL-17A⁺ and IL-22⁺ lymphocyte populations in the lamina
propria of Lrrc8aΔIEC mice (revised Fig. 8F–H; revised Fig. S12J–L). In addition,
updated metabolomic analyses revealed alterations in several bile acid species under
epithelial VRAC deficiency (revised Fig. S7G, H). We consider these bile acid
perturbations to be a consequence of disrupted epithelial zonation under IEC VRAC
deficiency. Although we cannot exclude the possibility that VRAC may directly
influence the transport of certain bile acids or related lipid metabolites, clarifying
whether VRAC contributes through direct permeability or indirect secondary
mechanisms will require future investigation.
Together, these new findings support a coherent mechanistic model in which
Lactobacillus supplementation enhances RA metabolism and restores enterocyte
zonation, thereby ameliorating epithelial–immune dysregulation in IEC VRAC-
deficient mice.
